summary:
Hatay Province stands under the national framework of Türkiye. The source inventory records no Hatay-specific incident, enforcement action, local ordinance or facility practice affecting trans visitors; the province is not distinguished from the national position.

Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence in Türkiye since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988. There is no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no direct discrimination protection for gender identity. Same-sex marriage is not recognised.

Openly LGBTQ people are barred from military service: conscripts who declare homosexuality are classified under a definition treating homosexuality as a 'psychosexual illness', must provide photographic proof, and risk their 'unfit report' leaking publicly.

Since October 2018 governors have extended event bans to LGBTI-focused gatherings generally. In June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and trans pride marches; police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful force, more than 90 people were arbitrarily detained, and prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches were still continuing at year's end. Istanbul pride had been banned repeatedly before that, with police dispersing the 2015 and 2016 parades using water cannon and tear gas, and the Istanbul, İzmir and Antalya prides all banned on 14 June 2019.

In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling that it had shared 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values' that could 'encourage or promote' LGBTI identities.

Amnesty International's Türkiye country report for 2025/26 records three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people made public during 2025, described as an unprecedented assault that would criminalise expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible. The packages were not submitted to parliament. A February 2026 press report separately stated the government was considering a law criminalising publicly encouraging 'behavior contrary to biological sex' with a sentence of one to three years; that provision was not included in the 2026 omnibus bill (the 12th judicial package).
tangentialFactors:
Hatay's position on the Syrian border places it within the corridor where Türkiye's general identity-document checks at transit points are most likely to be applied to a trans visitor carrying foreign ID whose presentation does not match its markers. The inventory records no Hatay-specific application of that check.

The national pattern of street-level stops of trans women for background checks, documented in Istanbul in August 2025, has no recorded Hatay counterpart in the sources; the province's exposure is inherited from the national framework rather than demonstrated locally.
localsOnly:
Trans residents of Hatay change legal gender under the national procedure available since 1988, but hold no statutory protection against discrimination on gender identity or sexual orientation and no recognition of same-sex marriage.

Residents serving in the military face the national bar on open service, the 'psychosexual illness' classification, the photographic-proof requirement and the risk of an 'unfit report' becoming public.

Local LGBTI+ associations and event organisers stand under the national pattern of governor-level bans on LGBTI-focused events since October 2018 and the December 2025 İzmir court dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association; no Hatay-specific association or event action appears in the inventory.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether any of the three 2025 draft law packages, or the February 2026 proposal on publicly encouraging 'behavior contrary to biological sex', has since been enacted is unresolved in the sources.

No Hatay-specific data on detentions, body searches, healthcare access for trans detainees, or local police practice was located; the province's position is stated only as standing under the national framework.

The inventory does not resolve whether hormone replacement therapy access, private-purchase cost or facility availability differs in Hatay from the national picture.
